original_question: Let A1A2...An be a polyhedron and let P be a point inside it. From P draw perpendiculars to each edge AiAj, and let Aij' be the foot of the perpendicular on the edge AiAj. Study the resulting edge pedal polyhedron and determine its geometric properties.
target_in_paper: Unsolved Problems 7, item 7.2: the 3D edge-pedal-polyhedron generalization of Problem 7 (the orthic/pedal construction, referred to nearby as Smarandache's Orthic Theorem).
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper's actual target. It correctly uses a polyhedron A1A2...An, an interior point P, perpendiculars from P to each edge A_iA_j, the feet A'_{ij}, and the name 'edge pedal polyhedron'; and it asks for the geometric properties of that object. It also silently repairs a typographical glitch in the paper by making clear that A'_{ij} is the foot on the edge A_iA_j.
missing_details: The paper's item is not an isolated problem: it is Unsolved Problem 7.2, posed specifically as a 3D extension of Problem 7 about the orthic triangle of an acute triangle.

The nearby planar source problem should be mentioned to preserve intent: Problem 7 studies the triangle formed by the feet of the altitudes of an acute triangle and proves an extremal result, summarized in Conclusion 1.

The ambient setting is ordinary Euclidean 3-space; this is implicit in the paper's elementary-geometry context. No algebraic data such as ring/field, homogeneity, degree, or nilpotency are relevant here.

The paper does not specify the combinatorial or incidence structure of the 'edge pedal polyhedron': there is one projection point for each edge, so the notation A1'A2'...An' is informal and not literally compatible with a general polyhedron.
For a stand-alone formulation, one should clarify whether the perpendicular from P is required to meet the edge segment itself rather than only the supporting line of that edge.

The triangle case assumes an acute triangle so the altitude feet lie on the sides; the 3D analogue does not state the corresponding condition on the polyhedron and the point P that guarantees a well-posed edge-pedal construction.

The phrase 'determine its geometric properties' remains open-ended in the paper; the nearby context indicates that the intended scope is the 3D analogue of the planar orthic/pedal construction from Problem 7, not an unrelated general theory of arbitrary projection polyhedra.
refined_question: In Euclidean 3-space, as a polyhedral analogue of Problem 7's orthic/pedal construction, let Q = A1A2...An be a polyhedron and let P be a point in its interior. For each edge A_iA_j of Q, let A'_{ij} be the orthogonal projection of P onto that edge. Regard the collection of all such feet as defining the edge pedal polyhedron of P with respect to Q. What geometric properties of this edge pedal polyhedron can be established as the 3-dimensional extension of the planar orthic/pedal configuration studied in Problem 7?
justification: The draft matches Unsolved Problem 7.2 almost verbatim: the paper asks, for a polyhedron A1A2...An and an interior point P, to draw perpendiculars from P to each edge A_iA_j, denote the feet by A'_{ij}, call the resulting object an edge pedal polyhedron, and ask what properties it has. The surrounding context matters: the paper's opening paragraph says the goal is to extend earlier 2D elementary-geometry problems from triangles to polygons or from 2D to 3D, and Problem 7 together with its conclusion provides the specific planar orthic/pedal model that 7.2 is meant to generalize. So the right refinement is not a broader question about arbitrary pedal solids, but a stand-alone restatement of Unsolved Problem 7.2 as the 3D edge-based extension of the orthic/pedal construction.
